claims.text: Conventional fusion-welding repair creates a risk of hot cracking in components with thermally sensitive microstructures.
Cold-sprayed high-hardness metallic or bimetallic coatings can restore damaged surfaces on high-value components.
Cold-sprayed coatings can delay surface-defect initiation relative to traditional fusion-weld repairs.
Cold-sprayed coatings can delay surface-defect initiation relative to untreated surfaces.
A tailored Ni-based superalloy or high-hardness stainless-steel powder is suitable for the proposed cold-spray repair.
Optimizing powder particle size and morphology promotes successful cold-spray coating deposition.
Cold spraying can produce a dense, well-adhered coating with a refined microstructure and low porosity.
The dense, adherent, refined, low-porosity coating preserves substrate integrity and resists surface-defect initiation.
Cold-spray deposition bonds particles through high-velocity impact, severe plastic deformation, and mechanical bonding without melting.
Avoiding melting prevents thermally induced substrate microstructural changes associated with hot cracking.
Cold-spray particle impact causes work hardening and grain refinement.
Work hardening and grain refinement increase surface hardness and wear resistance.
The cold-sprayed coating provides improved corrosion protection.
The cold-sprayed repair will have higher surface hardness than both fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
The cold-sprayed repair will have lower wear rates than both fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
The cold-sprayed repair will have lower corrosion rates than both fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
The proposed coating remains beneficial during extended exposure to corrosive environments at approximately 200°C.
Successful repair requires geometry that permits uniform coating application and effective particle impact.
Insufficient substrate adhesion or a powder composition poorly matched to the substrate can limit coating performance.
